newsitem.title: INDIA: U.S. balloonist says global flight within reach.
newsitem.headline: U.S. balloonist says global flight within reach.

text.p: Record-breaking U.S. adventurer Steve Fossett said on Tuesday that someone would fly around the world in a balloon within three years, but he declined to say if he would try his luck again.

Clean-shaven and rested after a night's sleep in a government guest house in northern India, Fossett said he would need at least another day to pack up his balloon, which snagged in a tree when he descended to earth on Monday.
The landing in a remote wheat field in the Ganges plain dashed his hopes of becoming the first balloonist to circle the globe without stopping.
But he said he was happy to have broken two ballooning records -- the greatest distance and longest time in the air -- before running short of fuel, and he called his aborted mission a success.

"There are a number of competing teams to try and make it around the world and I think one of them will succeed within three years," Fossett told Reuters outside the Kamla Nehru Institute of Technology guest house where he spent the night.
"My team has the most experience with this kind of flight. We certainly have a good chance of being the first person to do it," he said.
But he declined to say whether he himself would make a fresh bid. "I just have to reflect," he said.
Fossett was greeted by more than 100 curious villagers when he touched down on Monday -- six days, two hours and 49 minutes after taking off from the U.S. heartland.
"They were very helpful, very friendly, but you don't know how you're going to get the work done with 100 people around you," Fossett said.

Escorted by a half dozen police, he said he planned to return to the landing site on Tuesday to pull his torn balloon out of the tree, and would need at least another day before he could start heading back home, probably via Delhi.
Police cordoned off the remote site in Nonkhar village, about 20 km (12 miles) south of Sultanpur in rural Uttar Pradesh state, India's most populous province.
Nonkhar is some 550 km (330 miles) southeast of the Indian capital and more than 16,000 km (10,000 miles) from St Louis, Missouri, where he began his ascent on January 13.
Guards placed their cots underneath the balloon to take advantage of the hot air which continued to escape from the deflated bladder and provided warmth in the chill air.
Villagers who looked on said they were confused when they saw Fossett's 45-metre (150-foot) balloon descend, then took fright when he dropped a gas cylinder before landing.
"It was making such a hissing noise that people were naturally frightened," said Devidin Koeri, a village physician.
Fossett said it took him hours on Monday before he found a telephone with which to speak overseas, and that he had spoken to his wife in the United States.
"She was very, very happy. She was relieved that I didn't fall into the Atlantic," he said.

The 52-year-old commodities broker said he was in for a surprise when he had his first copious meal on Monday night. "They gave me a Chinese meal. I was expecting them to bring some Indian food," he said.
Dressed in a yellow pullover and grey trousers, Fossett said he was looking forward to some more rest.
"I would love to have a vacation now," he said. "That's a very good idea. Have a cocktail and watch television."
